Giulia has one long strand of spaghetti she needs to make smaller. Every time she breaks one piece of spaghetti, it becomes three pieces, as shown in the picture. Which of the following numbers of pieces could she not get?

solutions.title: Each break adds 2
solutions.body:
Giulia starts with 1 piece. When she breaks a piece, that one piece turns into 3 pieces, so she gains $3 - 1 = 2$ pieces.

So the number of pieces goes 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, ... It always goes up by 2, starting from 1, so it is always an **odd** number.

13, 17, 23 and 25 are odd, but 20 is even. She can never get 20 pieces.

**Answer: (C) 20**

solutions.title: Count the breaks
solutions.body:
After $b$ breaks she has $1 + 2b$ pieces. Check each choice:

- 13 pieces: $1 + 2 \times 6$, so 6 breaks.
- 17 pieces: $1 + 2 \times 8$, so 8 breaks.
- 20 pieces: $1 + 2b = 20$ means $2b = 19$, which isn't a whole number of breaks!
- 23 pieces: $1 + 2 \times 11$, so 11 breaks.
- 25 pieces: $1 + 2 \times 12$, so 12 breaks.

**Answer: (C) 20**

prompt: In the diagram, the square ABCD has side lengths of 10 cm. What is the area of the shaded part of the square?

Sixty tiles are laid in a long line.

- First, Adam removes every sixth tile.
- Next, Berta removes every fifth tile from the remaining tiles.
- Then, Caleb comes and removes every fourth tile from the remaining tiles.
- Finally, Doris removes all the remaining tiles.

How many tiles does Doris remove?

solutions.title: Step by step
solutions.body:
- Adam removes every sixth tile from 60 tiles: $60 \div 6 = 10$ tiles. That leaves $60 - 10 = 50$.
- Berta removes every fifth tile from 50: $50 \div 5 = 10$ tiles. That leaves $50 - 10 = 40$.
- Caleb removes every fourth tile from 40: $40 \div 4 = 10$ tiles. That leaves $40 - 10 = 30$.
- Doris removes the rest: **30** tiles.

**Answer: (C) 30**

solutions.title: Keep a fraction each time
solutions.body:
Removing every sixth tile keeps 5 out of every 6, removing every fifth keeps 4 out of every 5, and removing every fourth keeps 3 out of every 4. So the tiles left are

$$60 \times \frac{5}{6} \times \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{3}{4} = 60 \times \frac{3}{6} = 30.$$

(The 5s and 4s cancel out.) Doris removes these 30 tiles.

**Answer: (C) 30**

prompt: Five big elephants and four small ones are walking along a path, as shown. When they reach the junction, each elephant turns either to the left or to the right. Which of the following cannot be the situation after they all pass the junction?
Clara starts with the number 12 and follows the arrows shown in the right diagram while performing the operations using the rules shown in the left diagram. What number will she finish with?

solutions.title: Follow the path
solutions.body:
The rules say: down arrow ↓ means $\times 4$, right arrow → means $\times 2$, left arrow ← means $\div 2$, up arrow ↑ means $\div 4$.

Starting at 12, the arrows go ↓ → ↓ ← ↓ ← ↑ ← ↑ → ↑:

$12 \xrightarrow{\times 4} 48 \xrightarrow{\times 2} 96 \xrightarrow{\times 4} 384 \xrightarrow{\div 2} 192 \xrightarrow{\times 4} 768 \xrightarrow{\div 2} 384 \xrightarrow{\div 4} 96 \xrightarrow{\div 2} 48 \xrightarrow{\div 4} 12 \xrightarrow{\times 2} 24 \xrightarrow{\div 4} 6$

**Answer: (B) 6**

solutions.title: Count the arrows
solutions.body:
Count each kind of arrow on the path: 3 down arrows ($\times 4$ three times), 2 right arrows ($\times 2$ twice), 3 left arrows ($\div 2$ three times) and 3 up arrows ($\div 4$ three times).

The three $\times 4$ and three $\div 4$ cancel each other. Two $\times 2$ and two of the $\div 2$ also cancel. What is left over is one $\div 2$.

So Clara ends with $12 \div 2 = 6$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

prompt: The year 2022 is a special year because the digit 2 appears three times. This is the third time Eva the tortoise has lived through such a year with three identical digits. What is the youngest age that Eva could be by the end of 2022?

solutions.title: List the special years
solutions.body:
Go back from 2022 and look for years with three identical digits:

- 2022: three 2s ✓
- 2021, 2020, ..., 2001: none of these has three equal digits (for example, 2002 has two 2s and two 0s).
- 2000: three 0s ✓
- 1999: three 9s ✓
- Before that, the next one is 1911.

So the last three special years are 1999, 2000 and 2022. For 2022 to be Eva's third such year, she must have lived through 1999, so she was born in 1999 at the latest. Born at the very end of 1999, she turns 23 at the end of 2022.

**Answer: (D) 23**

solutions.title: Check the choices
solutions.body:
If Eva were 22 at the end of 2022, she was born in 2000. Then her special years would be just 2000 and 2022, only two of them. Ages 18 and 20 are even younger and give even fewer.

If she is 23, she was born in 1999, and her special years are 1999, 2000 and 2022: exactly three! So 23 is the youngest possible age.

**Answer: (D) 23**

prompt: A rectangular-based water tank has dimensions 1 m × 2 m × 4 m. It contains water to a depth of 25 cm, as shown in the left-hand picture. The tank is turned so that a 1 m × 2 m face becomes the base, as shown in the right-hand picture. What is the depth of the water now?

Jessi writes the seven numbers 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 in the circles in the picture so that the sums of the three numbers on each line are equal. What is the largest possible sum of three numbers on a line that Jessi can get?

solutions.title: Put the biggest number in the middle
solutions.body:
Each line is the middle circle plus two outer circles. The middle number is on all three lines, so making it big helps all three sums. Put 9 in the middle.

Now split 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 into three pairs with the same sum: $3 + 8 = 11$, $4 + 7 = 11$, $5 + 6 = 11$. 

Each line adds up to $9 + 11 = 20$.

**Answer: (E) 20**

solutions.title: Why it can't be more
solutions.body:
Add up all three lines. The outer numbers are each counted once, and the middle number is counted three times. All seven numbers add to $3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 9 = 42$. So the three lines together make $42 + 2 \times \text{middle}$.

The middle is at most 9, so the three lines add up to at most $42 + 18 = 60$. Each line is a third of that: at most $60 \div 3 = 20$. And 20 really works with 9 in the middle (pairs 3+8, 4+7, 5+6). Choices 28 and 22 are too big.

**Answer: (E) 20**

A, B, C and D are points on a line segment with AB = 7, BC = 5, CD = 8 and DA = 6. Which two points are at the beginning and at the end of this line segment?

solutions.title: Use a number line
solutions.body:
Put A at 0. Since AB = 7, put B at 7.

C is 5 away from B, so C is at 2 or 12. D is 6 away from A, so D is at 6 or −6.

CD must be 8. Try the options: C = 2 and D = −6 gives $2 - (-6) = 8$ ✓. (C = 2, D = 6 gives 4; C = 12, D = 6 gives 6; C = 12, D = −6 gives 18.)

So the points in order are D (−6), A (0), C (2), B (7). The ends are **B and D**.

**Answer: (C) B, D**

solutions.title: Check which point is between
solutions.body:
If a point sits between two others, the two short distances add up to the long one.

- $DA + AC$: we don't know AC yet, but $AB = 7$ and $BC = 5$ means C could be between A and B with $AC = 7 - 5 = 2$.
- Then $DA + AC = 6 + 2 = 8 = CD$ ✓, so A is between D and C.

The order is D, A, C, B: D to A is 6, A to C is 2, C to B is 5. Every given distance checks out: AB = 2 + 5 = 7, BC = 5, CD = 2 + 6 = 8, DA = 6. The ends are B and D.

**Answer: (C) B, D**

prompt: Some identical glasses are stacked on top of each other. A stack of 8 glasses is 42 cm high and a stack of 2 glasses is 18 cm high. How high is a stack of 6 glasses?

In the picture, each animal represents a positive integer and different animals represent different integers. The sum of the two integers in each column is written below that column. What is the largest possible sum of the four integers in the first row?

To unlock a given lock, you get the following four hints.

- 6 8 2: One of these digits is correct and in the right place.
- 6 1 4: One of these digits is correct but in the wrong place.
- 2 0 6: Two of these digits are correct but in the wrong place.
- 7 3 8: All of these digits are incorrect.

What is the correct code for the lock?

solutions.title: Rule out the choices
solutions.body:
- 7, 3 and 8 are not in the code. That rules out (B) 082.
- Hint 6 1 4 says its correct digit is in the **wrong** place. In (A) 604 and (C) 640, the 6 is first, just like in 6 1 4, so it would be in the right place. Rule out (A) and (C).
- Hint 6 8 2 needs one digit in the right place. In (E) 046, the 6 is last, not first, and there's no 8 or 2 in it. So nothing from 6 8 2 is in the right place. Rule out (E).

Only (D) 042 is left. Check it: 6 8 2 has the 2 in the right place ✓. 6 1 4 has the 4, but in the wrong place ✓. 2 0 6 has the 2 and the 0, both in the wrong places ✓. 7 3 8 has nothing ✓.

**Answer: (D) 042**

solutions.title: Build the code
solutions.body:
From 7 3 8, the digits 7, 3 and 8 are out. So in 6 8 2, the one correct digit (in the right place) is 6 in first place or 2 in last place.

If 6 were first, then in 6 1 4 the 6 would also be in the right place, but that hint says its correct digit is in the wrong place. So the 2 is last, and 6 is not in the code at all: _ _ 2.

In 2 0 6, two digits are correct. Since 6 is out, they are 2 and 0. The 0 is in the wrong place there (middle), so 0 goes first: 0 _ 2.

In 6 1 4, one digit is correct but in the wrong place. It isn't 6, and 1 would have to go in the middle, which is its own spot in 6 1 4. So it's 4, in the middle: **042**. It fits every hint.

**Answer: (D) 042**

prompt: Elena wants to place five different single-digit numbers in the five circles so that the number inside each triangle is the product of the three numbers on its vertices. What is the sum of the three numbers on the vertices of the shaded triangle?

solutions.title: Start in the middle
solutions.body:
The middle circle is a corner of all four triangles, so it divides 105, 84, 210 and 168. Break them into primes: $105 = 3 \times 5 \times 7$, $84 = 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 7$, $210 = 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7$, $168 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 7$. They all share 3 and 7.

Try middle = 7. Then the top and left multiply to $105 \div 7 = 15$, the top and right to $84 \div 7 = 12$, the left and bottom to $210 \div 7 = 30$, and the right and bottom to $168 \div 7 = 24$.

Top = 3 works: left = 5, right = 4, bottom = $30 \div 5 = 6$, and right × bottom = $4 \times 6 = 24$ ✓. All five numbers 7, 3, 5, 4, 6 are different single digits.

The shaded triangle has middle, right and bottom: $7 + 4 + 6 = 17$.

**Answer: (D) 17**

solutions.title: Compare neighbouring triangles
solutions.body:
The top two triangles share the top and middle circles, so the only difference is left vs right: left : right = 105 : 84 = 5 : 4. With single digits, left = 5 and right = 4.

The left two triangles share the left and middle circles, so top : bottom = 105 : 210 = 1 : 2. So bottom = 2 × top.

Now $\text{top} \times 5 \times \text{middle} = 105$, so top × middle = 21 = 3 × 7. Top can't be 7 (bottom would be 14), so top = 3, middle = 7 and bottom = 6.

Shaded triangle: $7 \times 4 \times 6 = 168$ ✓, and the sum is $7 + 4 + 6 = 17$.

**Answer: (D) 17**

prompt: Which of the following nets cannot be folded into the solid shown (a 2 × 1 × 1 box with two minus signs on the front, two bars on top and a plus sign on the end)?

solutions.title: Find the end squares
solutions.body:
The solid is a $2 \times 1 \times 1$ box. It has 4 long faces (each made of 2 squares) and 2 small square ends. On the solid, one of the **ends** has the + sign.

In net (B), the bottom row has two single squares that stick out on their own (one with a bar, one with a minus). They can't pair up with a neighbour to make a long face, so they must be the two ends. The rest of the net splits into long faces: bar-bar, plus-plus, minus-minus, minus-minus.

So in (B) the + signs are on a long face and neither end has a +. It can never fold into the solid.

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Fold a net that works, then compare
solutions.body:
Try net (A): its middle row is blank, minus, minus, plus, blank, blank, with two bar squares above the last two and two blank squares below the minus pair.

Fold it: the minus pair is the front, the plus square folds back to become the right end, and the last two blank squares become the back. The bar pair attached to the back folds over to make the top, with the bars running across, just like the solid. So (A) works.

Net (B) is different: its two + squares sit side by side as one long face, and the solid has no long face with plus signs. So (B) is the one that cannot be folded into the solid.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Joining small cubes of the same volume but of different material forms a rectangular box as shown in the figure. If each white cube weighs 2 grams and each grey cube weighs 1 gram, how many grams does the box in the figure weigh?

solutions.title: Weigh one stack
solutions.body:
The box is 5 cubes wide, 5 cubes deep and 6 cubes tall. The colours alternate like a chessboard, so going up any stack of 6 cubes the colours go white, grey, white, grey, white, grey (or grey first). Every stack has 3 white and 3 grey cubes.

One stack weighs $3 \times 2 + 3 \times 1 = 9$ grams. There are $5 \times 5 = 25$ stacks, so the box weighs $25 \times 9 = 225$ grams.

**Answer: (B) 225**

solutions.title: Count the colours
solutions.body:
The box has $5 \times 5 \times 6 = 150$ cubes. The height, 6, is even, so the colours split exactly in half: 75 white and 75 grey.

Weight: $75 \times 2 + 75 \times 1 = 150 + 75 = 225$ grams.

(A quick check: if all 150 cubes were grey, the box would weigh 150 g. The 75 white cubes each add 1 more gram, so $150 + 75 = 225$.)

**Answer: (B) 225**

prompt: The three pictures show a structure made from identical cubes as seen from the top, from the front and from the right. What is the maximum number of cubes that could have been used to build the structure?

Thirty people are sitting around a circular table. Some of them are wearing hats. Those who wear a hat always tell the truth, while those who do not wear a hat can either lie or tell the truth. Each person says: "At least one of my two neighbours is not wearing a hat." What is the greatest number of people who could be wearing a hat?

solutions.title: Groups of three
solutions.body:
A person with a hat tells the truth, so at least one of their neighbours has no hat. That means **three people with hats can never sit in a row**, because the one in the middle would have hats on both sides.

Split the 30 seats into 10 groups of 3 seats in a row. Each group has at most 2 hats, so there are at most $10 \times 2 = 20$ hats.

20 really works: go around the table hat, hat, no hat, hat, hat, no hat, ... Every hat-wearer sits next to a person without a hat, so they tell the truth. People without hats are allowed to say anything.

**Answer: (D) 20**

solutions.title: Each bare head helps at most two
solutions.body:
Every hat-wearer needs a neighbour without a hat. A person without a hat has only 2 neighbours, so they can "help" at most 2 hat-wearers.

If $h$ people wear hats, at least $h \div 2$ people must be hatless. So $h + h \div 2 \le 30$, which means $h \le 20$.

The pattern hat, hat, no hat repeated 10 times uses exactly 20 hats and 10 bare heads, and every hat-wearer is telling the truth. 25 would need at least 12.5 bare heads, but only 5 seats are left.

**Answer: (D) 20**
